sections.title: Foreword
sections.html:
This book is devoted to the blessings that we recite to the Lord our God. And although the Divine matter is high and exalted, great and awesome, through the blessings it envelops and fills our lives. Our Sages already said that one who wishes to be pious should be meticulous in his blessings (Bava Kamma 30a). Through the blessings a person merits to remember God in all his ways, and to add meaning and blessing to his own life and to the entire world.

And since the matter of blessings is great and vast, its details are very numerous, for through the principles and details of the laws of blessings we refine our lives to the utmost, so that they will accord with the Divine matter revealed in the world according to our comprehension. And through this we draw blessing into all the work of our hands.

In the past I already merited to write some of the laws of blessings, and they were printed in Likkutim 3. Therefore, I hoped that I would merit to complete the clarification of the rest of the laws of blessings within about a year. However, the more I tried to hurry, the longer things grew. Although at first glance the laws of blessings appear easy, in practice they are complex and complicated, in a certain respect more so than the laws of Shabbat and Pesaḥ. Almost every topic is connected and bound up with other topics, and there is great difficulty in defining each matter on its own, and afterward in defining it within the fabric of the rest of the laws. For example, the law of the final blessing depends on several variable factors: first, on the type of food, and there are foods composed of several foods, in which case it is necessary to define which is the primary one. Second, on the quantity eaten, and there is a difference between a drink and a food. Third, on the time over which it is eaten, for if it was eaten with breaks that are too long, one no longer recites the blessing. And each detail is composed of several laws. And if one moves to another place, the topic broadens to further questions: for which food will he need to return to his original place in order to recite the final blessing, and if he wishes to continue eating, for which food will he need to recite a first blessing again, etc.

In order to guide the public in the laws of blessings, many books have been written in recent years, each with merits of its own. In Yalkut Yosef, many topics were explained according to the rulings of the author's father, the Gaon, and in Halakha Berura his brother summarized the laws according to the order of the Shulḥan Arukh with great precision. In both, the laws follow the rulings of the Sephardim, who conduct themselves according to the Shulḥan Arukh and the Aḥaronim who follow in its footsteps. In Birkat Hashem, the author clarified the halakhic topics well and at length on the basis of the Rishonim, and ruled what emerges from them, in his view, for Sephardic customs. In Piskei Teshuvot, the author nicely summarized many responsa and opinions for practical application, following the order of the Shulḥan Arukh, mainly according to Ashkenazic rulings. The author of the book Ve-zot Ha-berakha merited to clarify many practical topics with several of the greatest halakhic authorities of the generation, Ashkenazim and also Sephardim, and in this he has a special merit. In Sha'arei Ha-berakha, the author arranged all the laws of blessings in meticulous detail, mainly according to Ashkenazic rulings. And many more books have been written on specific topics in the laws of blessings.

However, many times, because of the abundance of details, fine points and elaborations, the principles were lost, and when a Jew faces a question, if he has not learned countless laws by heart, he will not know how to act. And even if we wish to teach these laws to students, we will have difficulty, because of the numerous details and because of the differing customs among the communities. Therefore, there is a need to define the principles well, in which all the customs are equal, and from there to approach the details, for in this way the learning is truer and more straightforward. In addition, in this way it is easier to remember the details, since they flow in a straight and logical line from the principles. And only afterward, in the course of dealing with the details, should the differences in custom among the communities be defined. And sometimes, when one approaches the details from the principle, one finds that in truth there is no dispute among the communities on this; rather, their eating habits were different, and consequently they acted differently in practice, but on the question before us there is no difference between the customs of the communities. A further advantage of emphasizing the principles is that when there is a detail that has not yet been addressed, the learner can deduce on his own, on the basis of the principles, how it is proper to act, and he will very likely succeed in arriving at the halakha, at least according to some of the poskim (halakhic authorities).

And as we learned in the study hall of our master Rav Kook, of blessed memory, the root that precedes everything is the foundation of faith, from which the principles of halakha and its details flow. And if this is so for all the laws, all the more so for the laws of blessings, which express the connection between a person and his God. And indeed, when one delves into the idea of faith, one finds that it accords with the principles of halakha. Therefore, I opened the book with the foundations of faith and the reasons behind the laws of blessings, and I also mentioned them in the openings of many chapters.

In the course of writing the book I deliberated over how far it is right to elaborate in the notes. The deliberation grew stronger because the number of learned people engaged with Peninei Halakha has increased, asking, raising difficulties and commenting. And in order to answer what they might ask, I needed to elaborate more, but I found myself moving away from the original aim of Peninei Halakha: to explain the foundations and principles in clear and concise language. Therefore, in the middle of writing the book, I decided to publish an additional book, namely "Harḥavot (Expansions) to Peninei Halakha: Berakhot." Some of the expansions deal with the sources of the topic in the Talmud and the Rishonim, and some deal with less common laws. And some of them elaborate on the spiritual reason of the halakha. And since the idea for this arose in the middle of writing the book, there are laws for which expansions were written and some for which expansions were not written. And even in the laws on which expansions were written, sometimes I was brief and sometimes I was lengthy. And it is not my intention that the book of expansions be distributed together with the book Peninei Halakha, in order to distinguish between the important and primary book and the expansions, which are not arranged as a systematic book, but rather as a supplement for close students and for those who wish to further discuss and ask.

To further explain the value of emphasizing the study of the principles, through which one can remember and properly fulfill the halakha in practice, we must know that many times, because of the complexity of the halakha and the multitude of its details and fine points, many people do not succeed in knowing, actually and in practice, what the halakha is. So it is in all areas, and especially in the laws of blessings. It turns out that when they encounter a practical question, although they would like to act according to the halakha, since they do not remember all its details, they do not know how to fulfill it, and doubt gnaws at the heart. There are those who, as a result, frequently ask rabbis about every step they take, until religious life appears full of anxiety and lacking joy and natural faith. And in contrast, there are those who do not ask and become accustomed to living with doubts, and as a result come to belittle the careful observance of halakha, which harmonizes the great vision with practical life. The Rishonim already wrote that a doubtful sin is more severe than a certain sin (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona at the beginning of Berakhot). And we likewise find that when Ḥazal instituted an enactment, they took care that the public would be able to fulfill it. Therefore we must explain the halakha clearly, and try as much as possible not to pile on details that may blur the principle.

Wherever there are differences in custom among the communities, I have written the different customs. This is the place to note that the main thing our Sages instructed regarding preserving customs (Pesaḥim 50b; Yerushalmi Eruvin end of chapter 3) refers to customs that are well established among all the people of a given place or a given community, and not to what one needs to ask knowledgeable people about how they acted in such-and-such a place. And all the more so it does not refer to what rabbis who lived in that place wrote. Rather, in all the laws for which there is no clear and well-known custom, one should follow the accepted rules of halakhic decision-making: that the halakha follows the majority opinion, and that in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient. And in those laws, one should take into account all the poskim from all the communities. True, in the past, because of the distance between the exiles, the rabbis mainly took into account the poskim who lived in their surroundings, in their own generation or in previous generations. However, today, when all the tribes of Israel live together and learn together, one should take into account all the poskim from all the communities. It should also be added that, as will be explained in chapter 12, the rule that in cases of doubt regarding blessings we are lenient does not cancel customs, and in addition, some say that it does not apply in a case of double doubt (sfek sfeka). Therefore, sometimes even in a case of doubt, the opinion of the majority of poskim, as halakha and in practice, is to recite the blessing.

It is also common that because of various doubts, entire blessings have almost been abolished from among us, such as the blessings over sights, the Sheheḥeyanu blessing over joyous events, and Ha-tov Ve-hametiv over a second wine. And on these topics I have written according to the opinion of the overwhelming majority of the poskim, who ruled that these blessings should be recited, without being concerned for the opinion of the minority who were hesitant to recite them. First, because this is the main halakhic view. And there is another important reason: although one should take remote doubts into account, nevertheless when the doubt completely abolishes a blessing that the Sages instituted, one should not be so concerned about it. For we must be more careful not to abolish an enactment of the Sages than to be concerned about a doubt raised by one of the later poskim. And on this I lean on a great tree, my master and teacher Rav Tzvi Yehuda Kook, of blessed memory, who was accustomed to reciting rare blessings, such as Sheheḥeyanu upon seeing beloved friends and students, and "who establishes the boundary of the widow" over settlements in the Land, and the like, and he would say that the tendency to raise remote doubts in the laws of blessings expresses doubts in faith.

I thank God for granting me the merit to learn and teach in the yeshiva and in the community of Har Bracha. From the residents I learn about the halakhic questions that accompany their lives, and with the Torah scholars in the yeshiva, the older and the younger, I merit to clarify the reasoning and the definitions. And without this combination, the reasoning and the conclusions are not properly directed. For sometimes, from the clarification of a topic a certain conclusion seemingly emerges, and a great question arises among those sitting in the study hall: why do people not act as emerges from the topic? But when one is familiar with reality and with the questions that arise from it, one understands that in practice there are additional halakhic considerations which led to a different ruling. And so matters gradually become clarified.

This is the place to thank Rabbi Oren Matza and Rabbi Maor Kayam, who helped me greatly in clarifying the topics, and they are full partners in the writing of this book and of the book of expansions. Thanks also to Rabbi Yonadav Zar, who assisted with proofreading and comments and prepared the book for print, and together with R. Netanel Rosenstein compiled the index. I also thank R. David Wichner, who assisted with proofreading and enlightening comments. Thanks also to Rabbi Shlomi Badash and Rabbi Ze'ev Sultanovitch for their assistance with notes and comments. And to R. Binyamin Kniesbacher, R. Noam Alsheikh, and my son-in-law R. Ḥaggai Cohen, who assisted with proofreading, and together with them the rest of the yeshiva students who participated in the classes and took part in the proofreading. "And from my students more than all of them."

Offerings of thanks to my father and teacher, Rabbi Zalman Baruch Melamed, may he live a long and good life, head of Yeshivat Beit El and rabbi of the community, and to my mother and teacher, and to my dear wife; and may it be God's will that we merit to raise all our children to Torah, to mitzvot, to the wedding canopy and to good deeds, and may the Torah not depart from our mouths and the mouths of our offspring forever.

I would further like to thank all those engaged in holy work in building the yeshiva and printing the books: R. David Sa'adah, R. Yisrael Sa'adia and R. Ya'akov Weinberger. May it be the will of God, may He be blessed, to give them understanding and strength to succeed in their work and fulfill all the wishes of their hearts for good.

About five months ago, on 12 Iyar 5768, R. Uri Wexler, my daughter-in-law's grandfather, passed away suddenly. May this book be for the elevation of his soul. R. Uri was an upright, modest man, who greeted people with a cheerful face and performed acts of kindness. For decades he served as a gabbai and Torah reader. He loved the settlement of Shomron, and he came often to visit his daughter's family in Har Bracha. His father, R. Shmuel, was the good friend of my grandfather, Prof. Yosef Walk, of blessed memory. In time, the families were joined together through the wedding of their great-grandchildren. From this wedding R. Uri merited to see his eldest great-grandson.

May it be God's will that through the study and observance of the laws of blessings we merit the building of the Land, for blessing is connected to the Land of Israel, as it is stated (Devarim 8:10): "You shall eat and be satisfied, and you shall bless the Lord your God for the good land that He has given you." For through the blessings we reveal the holiness that is in the Land, and only in the Land of Israel is it possible to reveal holiness within physicality itself. And through this a great sanctification of God's name takes place, when it is revealed that even the food we eat and its good taste belong to matters of holiness. And this is what the Sages said (Sifrei): "For blessing depends only on the Land," as it is stated (Devarim 15:4): "For the Lord will surely bless you in the land that the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance to possess." And may it be God's will that through inheriting the Land and building it, we merit to complete the building of the Land with the building of the heart of the Land, which is Jerusalem, our holy and glorious city. And from Jerusalem may God draw down further blessing upon us, as it is stated (Tehillim 128:5): "May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life." For in Jerusalem it is possible to reveal how all the different hues do not contradict one another, but rather complement one another and add blessing to one another. And through this may we merit the building of the Holy Temple, and the resting of the Shekhina among us, and through this blessing will spread to us and to the entire world, "for as long as the service of the Holy Temple exists, the world is blessed for its inhabitants and the rains fall in their proper time" (Avot De-Rabbi Natan 4).

Eliezer Melamed

The Ten Days of Repentance, 5769

Ten years have passed since the printing of the first edition, and in the meantime two more editions have come out, and this is the fourth. I consider a new edition to be a printing that contains additional laws or further explanations of the halakha, but when there are corrections of precision, which are added from printing to printing, I do not consider it a new edition. In this edition several laws were indeed clarified, such as the Mezonot blessing over shalva (puffed wheat) and granola (6:13), and pat ha-ba'a be-kisnin (3:8; 6:2-4), and I relied more on those who hold that hearing through hearing aids is valid (12:9), and I added a clarification regarding the blessing on the birth of a daughter (17, note 11), and I expanded the clarification of the laws of Birkat Ha-gomel while taking into account changes in reality (chapter 16). In addition, a chapter was added on Tefilat Ha-derekh (the Traveler's Prayer), whose laws were previously brought in Likkutim (vol. 2, 10:6-10), and are now brought here with additional clarifications.

Eliezer Melamed

Ḥeshvan 5779

In this fifth edition, quite a number of matters were clarified in a clearer way, and rulings were also added, which arose following new questions or further clarification. In the course of this, the style was also polished and shortened, in accordance with the guidance of the Sages (Ḥullin 63b): "A person should always teach his student in a concise way."

Eliezer Melamed

Summer 5783
